1:1.t: Philemon was endowed with no dignity of ecclesiastical ordination, but was a praiseworthy man, one of the people. To him he writes a letter on behalf of Onesimus, his household slave, that he may not only pardon him but also give thanks to God, because he has received him back such that he should regard him not as a slave but as a most beloved brother.

Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy the brother, to Philemon the beloved brother and sharer with us in labours, and to Appia the dearest sister, and to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church in his house. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. To give dignity to the letter sent by him, he began from the indignity done to him. For just as to be bound because of sin is a reproach, so on the contrary to endure the chains of custody for Christ is the greatest glory; for at the time when he sent this letter he was in custody. Now although Philemon was not a cleric, yet for devotion's sake he took part in ecclesiastical needs, which is why he calls him a sharer in labours. For there are many who, though they are worthy, nevertheless excuse themselves, judging themselves too lowly for so great a ministry: whereby they appear truly worthy.

How many masters has he who has forsaken the One! But let us not forsake Him. Who would forsake Him Whom they follow bound with chains indeed, but chains of love, which set free and do not bind, those chains in which they who are bound boast, saying: "Paul the bondservant of Jesus Christ, and Timothy." It is more glorious for us to be bound by Him, than to be set free and loosed from others. Who then would flee from peace? Who would flee from salvation? Who would flee from mercy? Who would flee from redemption?

"Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ," saith he, "and Timothy the brother." Great is the designation of Paul: no title of principality and power, but he speaks of bonds and chains! Truly great indeed! Although many other things made him illustrious; his being caught up into the third heaven, his being transported to Paradise, his hearing unutterable words; yet he sets down none of these, but mentions the chain instead of all, for this made him more conspicuous and illustrious than these. And why so? Because the one were the free gifts of the Lord's lovingkindness; and the other the marks of the constancy and patience of the servant. But it is customary with those who love, to glory more in the things which they suffer for those who are beloved, than in the benefits they receive from them. A king is not so proud of his diadem, as Paul gloried in his chains. And very justly. For a diadem affords but an ornament to the crowned head; […]

These things are said to a master in behalf of a servant. Immediately at the outset, he has pulled down his spirit, and not suffered him to be ashamed, he has quenched his anger; calling himself a prisoner, he strikes him with compunction, and makes him collect himself, and makes it appear that present things are nothing. For if a chain for Christ's sake is not a shame but a boast, much more is slavery not to be considered a reproach. And this he says, not exalting himself, but for a good purpose doing this, showing thence that he was worthy of credit; and this he does not for his own sake, but that he may more readily obtain the favor. As if he had said, "It is on your account that I am invested with this chain." As he also has said elsewhere, there indeed showing his concern, but here his trustworthiness.

Nothing is greater than this boast, to be called "the stigmatized of Christ." "For I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus." (Gal. vi. 17.)

"The prisoner of the Lord." For he had been bound on His account. Who would not be struck with awe, who would not be humbled when he hears of the chains of Christ? Who would not be ready to give up even his own life, much less one domestic?

"And Timothy our brother."

He joins another also with himself, that he, being entreated by many, may the more readily yield and grant the favor.

"Unto Philemon our dearly beloved, and fellow-laborer."

If "beloved," then his confidence is not boldness nor forwardness, but a proof of much affection. If a "fellow-laborer," then not only may he be instructed in such a matter, but he ought to acknowledge it as a favor. For he is gratifying himself, he is building up the same work. So that apart from any request, he says, thou hast another necessity for granting the favor. For if he is profitable to the Gospel, and thou art anxious to promote the Gospel, then oughtest thou not to be entreated, but to entreat.

Those who refuse to receive among the Epistles of Paul the one which is written to Philemon say that the Apostle did not always, nor in all things, speak with Christ speaking in him. For, they argue, human weakness could not have borne the one unbroken course of the Holy Spirit; nor would the necessities of this poor body always be fulfilled in the presence of the Lord: such as arranging a meal, taking food, being hungry, being filled, digesting what has been taken in, replenishing what has been used up. I say nothing of the other things which they unfold in an elaborate and forced manner, so as to affirm that there was some time in which Paul would not dare to say: "I live, now not I, but Christ lives in me" (Gal. 2:20); and this: "Or do you seek a proof of him who speaks in me, Christ" (2 Cor. 13:3)? What sort of proof of Christ is it, they say, to hear: "The cloak which I left at Troas with Carpus, when you come bring with you" (2 Tim. 4:13)? […]

Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy the brother, to Philemon the beloved and our fellow worker, and to Apphia the sister, and to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church that is in your house: grace to you and peace from God our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.

You have been pleased to have me dictate to you on the Epistles of Paul in a back-to-front and inverted order. For when you, O Paula and Eustochium, often asked me to do it, and I stubbornly refused, you compelled me at least to discuss a short one, and one which seemed to you the last in sense and order as well as in the number of its verses. I shall therefore attempt at the end what belongs to the beginning. Another commentator would ask at once, in his introduction to the Apostle, why, or at what time, or by whose naming, he received the name of Paul in place of Saul. I am now compelled to do this, although before this day I had never dared to utter even a mu about him, as the saying goes. […]

According to the Jews, Paul means "admirable"; Timothy, "beneficent"; Philemon, "wonderfully gifted" or "mouth of bread", from os "mouth", not os "bone"; Apphia, "continent" or "liberty"; Archippus, "length of work"; Onesimus, "answering"; Epaphras, "fruitful" and "seeing", or "growing up"; Mark, "exalted by commandment"; Aristarchus, "mountain of greater work"; Demas, "silent"; Luke, "himself rising up". If you wish to understand these names according to their meaning, it is not difficult to see that the admirable and beneficent one writes above all to him to whom all faults have been forgiven and whose mouth lies open to the heavenly bread. Next he writes to the continent woman, the free woman, and to the length of work, because he never desists from holy labour. He writes on behalf of him who answers to his own testimony. He writes also that greeting is given to him to whom the Epistle is specially dedicated, by growing fruitfulness. […]

"Paul, a prisoner". Immediately from the opening words he instructs the master not to shame the servant. For all things, even chains, are good for Christ. And that it is right for grace to be given to the prisoner for Christ.

"and Timothy our brother". He includes Timothy as a partner in the supplication.

"to Philemon our beloved". If beloved, he will grant favor; if a coworker, he will not put the servant to shame in the service of the preaching. Onesimus, having been given, will also fulfill the work of the master Philemon.

"Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ." Straightaway from the very beginning he teaches the master not to be ashamed of his slave who has become a fellow slave. For on account of Christ all things are noble, even bonds, in which he himself also rejoices, so that he is even named after them. By this he strongly entreats, showing that it is only right to do a favor for one who is held in bonds for Christ.

"And Timothy the brother." As if considering himself not sufficient for the entreaty, he joins Timothy also as a fellow-petitioner, so that Philemon might yield to the request of many.

"Philemon, our beloved and fellow worker." If he is beloved, he will show mercy. If he is a fellow worker, he will not detain his servant, but will send him back again to the ministry of preaching, which he himself also serves. For the servant too will fulfill such a task of the master, if he is returned again.

1:2.t:
"And to our beloved Apphia."

It seems to me that she was his partner in life. Observe the humility of Paul; he both joins Timothy with him in his request, and asks not only the husband, but the wife also, and some one else, perhaps a friend.

"And Archippus," he says, "our fellow-soldier."

Not wishing to effect such things by command, and not taking it ill, if he did not immediately comply with his request; but he begs them to do what a stranger might have done to aid his request. For not only the being requested by many, but the petition being urged to many, contributes to its being granted. And on this account he says, "And Archippus our fellow-soldier." If thou art a fellow-soldier, thou oughtest also to take a concern in these things. But this is the Archippus, about whom he says in his Epistle to the Colossians, "Say to Archippus, Take heed to the ministry which thou hast received in the Lord, that thou fulfill it." (Col. iv. 17.) It seems to me too, that he, whom he joins with him in this request, was also one of the Clergy. And he calls him his fellow-soldier, that he may by all means cooperate with him.

"And to the Church in thy house."

Here he has not omitted even the slaves. For he knew that often even the words of slaves have power to overthrow their master; and more especially when his request was in behalf of a slave. And perhaps it was they particularly who exasperated him. He does not suffer them therefore to fall into envy, having honored them by including them in a salutation with their masters. And neither does he allow the master to take offense. For if he had made mention of them by name, perhaps he would have been angry. And if he had not mentioned them at all, he might have been displeased. Observe therefore how prudently he has found a way by his manner of mentioning them, both to honor them by his mention of them, and not to wound him. For the name of the "Church" does not suffer masters to be angry, even though they are reckoned together with their servants. For the Church knows not the distinction of master and servant. By good actions and by sins she defines the one and the other. […]

They write also to Apphia the sister, who had in her nothing of a false and feigned sisterhood. And they write to Archippus the fellow soldier: I think that, fighting with Paul and Timothy against adversaries for the name of Christ, he proved victorious, and is therefore now called fellow soldier because he prevailed in the same contest and war. It is written also to the church that is in his house. But this is ambiguous: is it the church in the house of Archippus, or the one in the house of Philemon? It seems to me that it should be referred not to the person of Archippus but to that of Philemon, to whom the epistle itself is assigned. For although Paul and Timothy write jointly to Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the church, yet what follows proves that Paul alone is writing to Philemon, one conversing with one: "I give thanks to my God always, and making remembrance of you". […]

"and to Apphia our beloved, and Archippus". Perhaps Apphia was the wife of Philemon, and Archippus. But see the humility, for it also urges these to join in the supplication.

"our fellow soldier". If a fellow soldier, he also struggles in this. This is the one about whom he writes to the Colossians: Tell Archippus, "Take heed to the ministry which you have received." (Co. 4:17)

"and to the church in your house". He invites the whole household, and slaves.

"And to Apphia, (our) beloved (sister), and to Archippus, our fellow soldier." Perhaps Apphia was the wife (of Philemon), and Archippus a friend. If he is a fellow soldier, then he will take part in this as well. This was the very same (Archippus) about whom he writes in the Epistle to the Colossians: "Say to Archippus, Take heed to the ministry which thou hast received" (Col. 4:17).

"And your household church." The apostle calls "church" all the believers in the house (of Philemon), including even the slaves. Notice the humility — he appeals to them as well, so that they might assist him in his request.

1:3.t:
"Grace to you, and peace."

By mentioning "grace," he brings his own sins to his remembrance. Consider, he says, how great things God has pardoned in thee, how by grace thou art saved. Imitate thy Lord. And he prays for "peace" to him; and naturally: for it comes then when we imitate Him, then grace abides. Since even that servant who was unmerciful to his fellow-servants, until he demanded the hundred pence, had the grace of his master abiding on him. But when he made that demand, it was taken from him, and he was delivered to the tormentors.

As for his saying, Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, it is still written by two to several. In almost all the Epistles the opening is the same, calling down upon them grace and peace from God the Father and Christ the Lord. From this it is shown that the nature of the Son and of the Father is one, since the Son can bestow what the Father bestows, and the Father is said to bestow what the Son bestows. Now grace is that by which we are saved through no merit or work. Peace is that by which we have been reconciled to God through Christ, as in the passage: "We beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God" (2 Cor. 5:20).
"Grace to you". How then will the grace of God be with you? If you also forgive those who owe you. How then is peace? If you are reconciled to the servant.
In what way will the grace of God be with us? If we too forgive our debtors. And in what way will there be peace? If you too are reconciled with your servant.

1:4.t: I give thanks to my God, always making mention of you in my prayers, hearing of your faith and love which you have towards the Lord Jesus and towards all the saints; that your sharing may become acceptable in the acknowledgement of every good that is in us in Christ. He says that he rejoices and gives thanks to God in his prayers, because Philemon was firm in faith and pressed on in good works: for he who loves Christ ought to prove this towards his servants, knowing that the Lord will reckon to himself whatever is shown to have been spent on his servants.

He does not immediately at the commencement ask the favor, but having first admired the man, and having praised him for his good actions, and having shown no small proof of his love, that he always made mention of him in his prayers, and having said that many are refreshed by him, and that he is obedient and complying in all things; then he puts it last of all, by this particularly putting him to the blush. For if others obtain the things which they ask, much more Paul. If coming before others, he was worthy to obtain, much more when he comes after others, and asks a thing not pertaining to himself, but in behalf of another. Then, that he may not seem to have written on this account only, and that no one may say, "If it were not for Onesimus thou wouldest not have written," see how he assigns other causes also of his Epistle. In the first place manifesting his love, then also desiring that a lodging may be prepared for him.

I give thanks to my God always, making remembrance of you in my prayers, hearing of your love and the faith which you have in the Lord Jesus and in all his saints: that the sharing of your faith may become evident in the full knowledge of every good which is in you in Christ.

These words he now speaks not as Paul and Timothy to Philemon and the rest, but as Paul alone to Philemon alone: I give thanks, he says, to my God always making remembrance of you in my prayers. It is said ambiguously, however, whether he gives thanks to his God always, or makes remembrance of him in his prayers always. And both can be understood. For he who instructs others to give thanks to God in all things can be hemmed in by no straits so tight that he does not himself render thanks to God always. […]

If ever "I" make "mention of you", I always do, "I give thanks to God" for you. Why? "Hearing of your love and faith", he says. Do you see that he does not immediately seek favor from the beginning?

"hearing of your love". which, if it were not great, would by no means be heard from Phrygia all the way to Rome.
Every time, he says, I remember you – and I remember you always when I pray – so many times I thank God for your virtue. What this virtue is, he explains further.

1:5.t:
"Hearing," he says, "of thy love."

This is wonderful, and much greater than if being present he had seen it when he was present. For it is plain that from its being excessive it had become manifest, and had reached even to Paul. And yet the distance between Rome and Phrygia was not small. For he seems to have been there from the mention of Archippus. For the Colossians were of Phrygia, writing to whom he said, "When this Epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the Church of the Laodiceans, and that ye likewise read the Epistle from Laodicea." (Col. iv. 16.) And this is a city of Phrygia.

And concerning the love which he had in Christ Jesus and in all his saints, the interpretation is indeed not difficult: it is the love by which, after God, we bid [men] to love our neighbors too. Now the question is this: how can anyone have the same faith in Christ Jesus and in his saints? For, by ἀπὸ κοινοῦ, the phrase sounds both ways: the love which you have in the Lord Jesus and in all his saints, and the faith which you have in the Lord Jesus and in all his saints. To expound this passage let us take an example from Exodus: "The people believed God and Moses his servant" (Exod. 19). One and the same belief is directed to Moses and to God, so that the people who believed in the Lord is said to have believed equally in the servant. And this holds not only in Moses but in all his saints, so that whoever has believed God cannot receive faith in him in any other way unless he also believes in his saints. For that love and faith toward God is not perfect which is thinned by hatred and unbelief toward his ministers. […]

Here he praises him for his goodness. From Phrygia it would not have been heard in Rome about his love and faith, if it had not been great. Since you love all the saints, that is, the faithful, you should also love Onesimus, for he too is now a believer — so that through this you may show yourself as one who loves the Lord as well. Do you see what compelling thoughts he gathers in his mind toward the fulfillment of the request?

1:6.t: The Apostle, however, says that he adds this to his prayers, that his working may be done with knowledge of goodness; that is, that he may do this work with such a mind as to expect the reward of it in the future.

I pray, he says, "that the communication of thy faith may become effectual in the knowledge of every good thing which is in Christ Jesus." Dost thou see him first giving, before he receives, and before he asks a favor himself bestowing a much greater one of his own? "That the communication of thy faith," he says, "may become effectual by the acknowledging of every good thing which is in you in Christ Jesus"; that is, that thou mayest attain all virtue, that nothing may be deficient. For so faith becomes effectual, when it is accompanied with works. For "without works faith is dead." (Jas. ii. 26.) And he has not said, "Thy faith," but "the communication of thy faith," connecting it with himself, and showing that it is one body, and by this particularly making him ashamed to refuse. If thou art a partaker, he says, with respect to the faith, thou oughtest to communicate also with respect to other things.

He who has equal love and faith in God and in his saints ought to have a sharing of that faith which is not unequal: so that as he believes and loves, so he may complete his love and faith in deed. Hence he says: May become evident in the full knowledge of every good; or, as it stands better in the Greek, "effective". For ἐνεργής can properly be rendered effective or operative: so that we may not merely believe that faith and love in God and in his saints can suffice for us, but that what we believe may be fulfilled in deed. It can happen, however, that someone has faith and completes it in deed, but simply and barely, without having full knowledge or knowledge of it, according to that saying of the Apostle: "I confess that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge" (Rom. 10:2). There are today many among the simple who do works of righteousness and have no knowledge of the things they themselves do. […]

"that the fellowship of your faith". It unites him to himself, just as if he said: Fellowship of faith is that which makes one and common. But why do you give thanks to God? So "that the" "fellowship of your faith", he says, "may become effective". But how will it be effective? If it proceeds to every work of virtue. Blessed Paul interprets himself. But how will it be "effective"? By this, that you have "the knowledge" and accomplish "every good thing".

"that is in us". He says that which is now also in us. (Matt. 25:40)

"for Christ Jesus". For whoever does good to someone, does it to Christ, especially to the saints.

I thank, says the apostle, God for your love, praying also that your faith, which you have in common with us, may be effective — active and living in your knowledge of every good work, that is, that you may love it and put it into practice. For faith is alive when we are diligent in every good work, just as it is dead when it is without good works. He added "which is in you" to show that even now Philemon already has every good work in himself, as if saying: (in the knowledge) of every good work even now in you, that is, already existing in you. Having said "the communion of faith," St. Paul unites Philemon with himself and makes them one. The faith is common and unifying, so that you must also be of one mind with me. Or by the communion of faith he means almsgiving, which comes from great faith. […]

1:7.t: For I have had great joy and consolation over your love, because the hearts of the saints have found rest through you, brother. It is plain that he indicates that he is glad for this reason, that Philemon was supplying necessities for the needs of the saints: hence he rejoices the more, being sure from this that he would also obey the commands of him who, it is agreed, is the greater.

Nothing so shames us into giving, as to bring forward the kindnesses bestowed on others, and particularly when a man is more entitled to respect than they. And he has not said, "If you do it to others, much more to me"; but he has insinuated the same thing, though he has contrived to do it in another and a more gracious manner.

"I had joy," that is, thou hast given me confidence from the things which thou hast done to others. "And consolation," that is, we are not only gratified, but we are also comforted. For they are members of us. If then there ought to be such an agreement, that in the refreshing of any others who are in affliction, though we obtain nothing, we should be delighted on their account, as if it were one body that was benefited; much more if you shall refresh us also. […]

For we have had great joy and consolation in your love, because the bowels of the saints have found rest through you, brother.

He drives home and explains more fully why he had said: "I give thanks to my God, always making remembrance of you in my prayers". For it was indeed fitting to give thanks to God for the love of Philemon, who, by receiving them, had refreshed the inner affection of the heart and the deep recesses of the saints' souls. And this is an apostolic idiom: he always says "bowels" when he wishes to show the full love of the mind. Therefore, rejoicing with those who rejoice, and believing that he himself had been refreshed along with those who had found rest, he has a joy that is not passing and light, nor such as might come about by chance. It is great, and as surpassing as the love that was in Philemon. That joy was increased by the consolation over Philemon's love, a consolation coming down, full, from the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation.

"we have great joy". Not only, Paul says, did we rejoice, but such was the pleasure that it even brought us comfort while in bonds.

"because the hearts of the saints". See! He wishes to say: If you grant favors to others, much more grant them to me; thus he does not say; but otherwise more skillfully. For he knows the memory of benefits done to others makes those who are urged more obedient.

"have been refreshed through you". For, Paul says, they find rest in your love. They rest because of you. Since you are such a one toward the saints as to also give them rest, I have the boldness to command you. Having boldness because of Christ; to command you a fitting thing; for this is what is proper. But I said to command, not because I rule over you, but because of the love which I love you and am loved by you, I seem to command, but I do not command. For even if I appear to command you, it is out of love that I do not command but rather encourage. Thus, I do the matter with great regard. […]

That is, we have joy, and not only joy, but also great consolation in bonds on account of your love, that is, your compassionate and generous disposition of heart.

Very wisely the apostle undertakes the matter, reminding him of his benefactions to others, in order to soften him all the more, while he considers that if he gives to others, to strangers, then all the more he ought to do this for Paul, his teacher. And he did not simply say: "you give to the saints," but you refresh "the hearts of the saints," that is, that they wholeheartedly receive your kindness, as it is offered to them generously and with comforting hospitality.

1:8.t: I do not issue orders to you, as if I were some great person. For though I am bound for the name [of Christ], I am not yet perfect in Jesus Christ. For now I begin to be a disciple, and I speak to you as fellow-disciples with me. For it was needful for me to have been stirred up by you in faith, exhortation, patience, and long-suffering. But inasmuch as love suffers me not to be silent in regard to you, I have therefore taken upon me first to exhort you that ye would all run together in accordance with the will of God. For even Jesus Christ, our inseparable life, is the [manifested] will of the Father; as also bishops, settled everywhere to the utmost bounds [of the earth], are so by the will of Jesus Christ.
1:8.s: Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians

1:8.t: Wherefore, though I have much confidence in Christ to command you what is fitting, yet for love's sake I rather beseech you, since you are such a one as Paul, an old man: but now also a prisoner of Christ Jesus. As far as reason required, it was fitting for the teacher to command the disciple out of confidence in his apostolic authority; but because Philemon was a good man, he calls him to obey through affection, as being of the same age, and a prisoner of Christ Jesus, that is, bound to the business of the Lord, or subjected to chains for his name, as the apostles themselves also were. For such were Judas and Silas, who, though they were of the people, were leading men among the brethren and had bound themselves to the works of the Lord (Acts 15:22 ff.), so that together with the apostolic men they might contend jointly for the faith of God. Hence Silas is found to be a sharer in the labours of the Apostle.

Observe how cautious he is, lest any of the things which were spoken even from exceeding love should so strike the hearer, as that he should be hurt. For this reason before he says, "to enjoin thee," since it was offensive, although, as spoken out of love, it was more proper to soothe him, yet nevertheless from an excess of delicacy, he as it were corrects it by saying, "Having confidence," by which he implies that Philemon was a great man, that is "Thou hast given confidence to us." And not only that, but adding the expression "in Christ," by which he shows that it was not that he was more illustrious in the world, not that he was more powerful, but it was on account of his faith in Christ,-then he also adds, "to enjoin thee," and not that only, but "that which is convenient," that is, a reasonable action. And see out of how many things he brings proof for this. Thou doest good to others, he says, and to me, and for Christ's sake, and that the thing is reasonable, and that love giveth...

Wherefore, having much confidence in Christ Jesus to command you what is profitable for love's sake, I rather beseech, since you are such a one, as Paul an old man, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.

Many praises of Philemon have been set out beforehand. The matter for which he is asked is also such as to be useful both to the one who grants it and to the one who asks. Paul therefore could have commanded rather than requested. This came from that confidence: one who had accomplished such great works for Christ's sake could surely not be unequal to himself in other matters. But he prefers to ask rather than to order, having first set forth the great authority of the one who asks, by which it is at once the Apostle who beseeches, and an old man, and a prisoner of Jesus Christ. Now the whole matter for which he asks is this. Onesimus, Philemon's slave, heaping theft upon flight, had pilfered certain things belonging to the household. […]

"Paul". And this alone is sufficient to persuade,

"the aged, but now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ". Do you see the motives for persuading?

Since, he says, you are such toward all the saints, that their hearts are refreshed by you, all the more I in Christ, that is, as having begotten you in Christ, I had boldness to command you, not as your master, but out of the love which I have for you and you for me. "That which is fitting," either — he commands you what is fitting, that is, that you fulfill what I need; or — that you honor all the saints: therefore I also, in accordance with what is fitting, that is, what falls to my lot, I had boldness to command you, yet I beseech. For I have such a necessary matter as to entreat you.

1:9.t: He is called younger still, who had not yet reached the mature age of the white-haired faith, who had not yet grown into a perfect man, into that full measure of the age of the fullness of Christ (Eph. IV, 13). Finally, he is only called young there (Acts VII, 57), where he was keeping the garments of those stoning Stephen. And for this reason, he desired Philemon to be like him not in his youth but in his old age, as he wrote: I beg you even more, now that I am old like Paul (Philem. 9). Therefore, he advises that younger widows should be avoided (I Tim. V, 11), not because of their age but because of a certain lasciviousness of youthful transgressions and immaturity of virtue. However, there is greater praise for chastity in a young person than in an old person.

As if he had said, I know indeed that I can effect it by commanding with much authority, from things which have already taken place. But because I am very solicitous about this matter, "I beseech thee." He shows both these things at once; that he has confidence in him, for he commands him; and that he is exceedingly concerned about the matter, wherefore he beseeches him.

"Being such an one," he says, "as Paul the aged." Strange! how many things are here to shame him into compliance! Paul, from the quality of his person, from his age, because he was old, and from what was more just than all, because he was also "a prisoner of Jesus Christ."

For who would not receive with open arms a combatant who had been crowned? Who seeing him bound for Christ's sake, would not have granted him ten thousand favors? By so many considerations having previously soothed his mind, he has not immediately introduced the name, but defers making so great a request. […]

As there are chains of coercion, so too there are chains of love, as the Lord says: "I drew them with chains of love." For indeed great are these chains, and chains of ineffable love, for those who are bound with them rejoice in their fetters. Do you want to know whether this is true? Hear how the Apostle Paul exults and rejoices in his chains, when he says: "I therefore a prisoner in the Lord beseech you." And again: "I beseech thee, whereas thou art such an one as Paul the aged, and now a prisoner also of Jesus Christ." You see how he rejoiced in the dignity of his chains, by the example of which he actually stirred up others. But there can be no doubt that where there is single-minded love of the Lord, there is also single-minded delight in chains worn for the Lord's sake: as it is written: "But the multitude of the believers was of one heart and one soul."
1:9.s: The Seven Books on the Incarnation of the Lord, Book 4, Chapter 11

1:9.t: Being such an ambassador, he says, I am worthy of being heard, as befits Paul the aged, that is, one who has authority both by virtue of his teaching dignity and by his age, and who has now received yet another, more important distinction — namely, being in chains for Christ. Do you see how many grounds for persuasion there are?

1:10.t: When slaves who are under the yoke flee to the brotherhoods, they should be admonished and made better, and then restored to their masters. So doing we imitate the blessed Paul, who, though he had begotten Onesimus through the gospel, yet sent him back to Philemon, persuading the servant that the yoke of slavery borne in a manner well pleasing to the Lord renders him worthy of the Kingdom of heaven, and exhorting the master not only to forbear his threats against Onesimus, remembering the words of his true Master: “If ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive your trespasses,” but also to have kinder feelings towards him—writing thus: “For perhaps he was therefore parted from thee for a season, that thou shouldest have him for ever, no longer as a servant, but more than a servant, a brother beloved.”

I beseech you for my son, whom I begot in chains, Onesimus, once unprofitable to you, but now very profitable to you and to me, whom I have sent back to you. Do you receive him as my own heart: whom I had wished to keep with me, that he might minister to me in your stead in the chains of the Gospel; but without your counsel I wished to do nothing, so that your good might not be as it were of necessity, but voluntary. It is no great thing for a humble man to bow himself, but it is praiseworthy for an exalted man to humble himself; therefore the Apostle asks one whom he has power to command, so as to be a pattern in all things for the advancement of merits. Onesimus, then, a fugitive who ran back to divine help, the Apostle baptized when he was in custody in the city of Rome (Acts 28:16), seeing in him the hope of usefulness.

And mark, on the other hand, the fervency of Paul also. Bound, scourged, thus he preached the Gospel. Oh, that blessed chain, with how great travail did it travail that night, what children did it bring forth! Yea of them too may he say, "Whom I have begotten in my bonds." Mark thou, how he glories, and will have the children thus begotten, to be on that account the more illustrious! Mark thou, how transcendant is the glory of those bonds, in that they give lustre not only to him that wore them, but also to them who were on that occasion begotten by him. They have some advantage, who were begotten in Paul's bonds, I say not in respect of grace, (for grace is one and the same,) nor in respect of remission, (for remission is one and the same to all,) but in that they are thus from the very outset taught to rejoice and to glory in such things.

Again the chains are mentioned to shame him into compliance, and then the name. For he has not only extinguished his anger, but has caused him to be delighted. For I would not have called him my son, he says, if he were not especially profitable. What I called Timothy, that I call him also. And repeatedly showing his affection, he urges him by the very period of his new birth, "I have begotten him in my bonds," he says, so that on this account also he was worthy to obtain much honor, because he was begotten in his very conflicts, in his trials in the cause of Christ.

I beseech you for my son, whom I have begotten in chains, Onesimus, who was once unprofitable to you, but now is profitable both to you and to me: whom I have sent back to you. But do you receive him, that is, my bowels, whom I had wished to keep with me, so that in your stead he might minister to me in the chains of the Gospel.

Wishing to obtain what he asks, he declares that he is now pleading not for Philemon's slave but for his own son, and for that son whom he had begotten in the chains of the Gospel, that is, the chains he was enduring for the Gospel of Christ. Before, this man had been unprofitable only to his master (for a slave who is a thief and a runaway has harmed no one but his master). Now, on the contrary, he is useful to his master himself and to Paul, and through Paul to the rest. By this compensation of usefulness he deserves more love than he had before deserved hatred. Hence he says: Who was once unprofitable to you. To you, he says, alone, not to the rest; […]

Paul mentions Philemon first, praising the servant as a beloved child, because he says he also baptized him. For this is the one, "I have begotten while in my chains." Therefore, having calmed his anger through these things, he thus gives the name "Onesimus", he says.

He has not yet mentioned the name of the one on whose behalf he is interceding. He first softens Philemon with praise of the servant, calling him his son. Why does he call him so? Because, he says, I begot him, that is, I instructed him with the Gospel and commanded that the one who believed be baptized, and this in difficult circumstances: in chains. Having thus softened his heart, he finally mentions the name.

1:11.t: He commends him in such a way as to signify his own mind towards him: that from unprofitable he has been made fit for worldly as well as divine services.

See how great is his prudence, how he confesses the man's faults, and thereby extinguishes his anger. I know, he says, that he was unprofitable.

"But now" he will be "profitable to thee and to me."

He has not said he will be useful to thee, lest he should contradict it, but he has introduced his own person, that his hopes may seem worthy of credit, "But now," he says, "profitable to thee and to me." For if he was profitable to Paul, who required so great strictness, much more would he be so to his master.

"formerly useless to you". For he knows that the acknowledged sin is to extinguish the master's anger.

"but now indeed useful both to you and to me". If such faithfulness is useful to Paul, who demands so much, it is clearly also useful to Philemon.

"He was once useless to you." He knows that confession of sin extinguishes wrath; therefore he speaks thus.

"But now is useful both to you and to me; I am sending him back." Since he became pious and holy, and therefore, he says, he is useful to both of us. If he is useful to Paul, who requires such great zeal, then certainly to Philemon as well. At the same time, he also implies that if he is useful to me, then he ought to be sent back to me. That is, I hand him over to you; use him as you wish. By handing him over, he all the more appeases his anger.

1:12.t:
By this also he has quenched his anger, by delivering him up. For masters are then most enraged, when they are entreated for the absent, so that by this very act he mollified him the more.

"Thou therefore receive him, that is mine own bowels."

And again he has not given the bare name, but uses with it a word that might move him, which is more affectionate than son. He has said, "son," he has said, "I have begotten" him, so that it was probable he would love him much, because he begot him in his trials. For it is manifest that we are most inflamed with affection for those children, who have been born to us in dangers which we have escaped, as when the Scripture saith, "Woe, Barochabel!" and again when Rachel names Benjamin, "the son of my sorrow." (Gen. xxxv. 18.)

"Thou therefore," he says, "receive him, that is mine own bowels." He shows the greatness of his affection. He has not said, Take him back, he has not said, Be not angry, but "receive him"; that is, he is worthy not only of pardon, but of honor. Why? […]

As for his saying: But do you receive him, that is, my bowels, this is what I said a little earlier: bowels signify the inner affection of the heart and a full and heartfelt will, when the one who is asked receives everything whatever that is in us. Otherwise, all children are the bowels of their parents.

"whom I have sent back". To hand Onesimus over to the master, rather extinguished his anger.

"to receive him as my very heart". What do I mean by "receive him"? Receiving this one, you will receive my own very "heart". Thus he says, I love him as one calls him his own "heart". And "receive" means to accept with love.
That is, receive him with love, or rather not him, but my very heart, for so much do I love him and carry him in my soul.

1:13.t: Dost thou see after how much previous preparation, he has at length brought him honorably before his master, and observe with how much wisdom he has done this. See for how much he makes him answerable, and how much he honors the other. Thou hast found, he says, a way by which thou mayest through him repay thy service to me. Here he shows that he has considered his advantage more than that of his slave, and that he respects him exceedingly.

"so that he might serve me in the chains of the gospel on your behalf". Do you see that Paul has brought the master to the very place, little by little? For he says that "he serves me on your behalf". Here he shows that he wishes what is more advantageous for the master. For if you say that you ought to serve, and he does this instead of you, the benefit is yours.

"in the chains of the gospel". In chains for the sake of the Gospel.

Pay attention to the wisdom of the apostle, how he gradually placed him (the servant) in the position of the master. "That in thy stead," he says, "he might minister unto me." He also shows that he desires the benefit of the master. If, he says, you are obligated to minister to me, and he does this in your stead, then clearly this is gain for you.

1:14.t: This particularly flatters the person asked, when the thing being profitable in itself, it is brought out with his concurrence. For two good effects are produced thence, the one person gains, and the other is rendered more secure. And he has not said, That it should not be of necessity, but "as it were of necessity." For I knew, he says, that not having learnt it, but coming to know it at once, thou wouldest not have been angry, but nevertheless out of an excess of consideration, that it should "not be as it were of necessity."

But without your counsel I wished to do nothing, so that your good might not be as it were of necessity, but voluntary.

The question asked by very many, and very often taken up again, is why God, in making man, did not create him good and upright. It can be resolved from the present passage. For if God is good voluntarily, and not of necessity, then in making man he ought to have made him after his own image and likeness, that is, so that man too would be good voluntarily, and not of necessity. But those who assert that he ought to have been made such that he could not admit evil are saying this: he ought to have been made such that he would be good by necessity, and not by will. Yet if he had been made such as to accomplish good not by will but by necessity, he would not be like God, who is good because he wills it, not because he is compelled. From this it is manifest that they are demanding two things contrary to each other. […]

"without your consent". This was especially humiliating for him, that he did not do something so necessary for him without your consent.

"so that your good deed would not be forced but voluntary". Paul did not say, "By force," but, "would not be forced;" as if he had said, "I knew that even against your will, forcing Onesimus on you, I would not cause you pain. But so that it may not seem to be done by force, I was not willing," he says.

And by this he softens Philemon most of all. The matter was so necessary: in chains, and moreover for God's sake, he intended to serve him; however, the apostle did not want to do this against Philemon's will. Therefore, should one not show mercy to him who could have made use of it himself, but did not want to?

He did not say: by necessity, but: "as it were by necessity," as if saying: of course, even by keeping him against your will, I would not truly have grieved you; nevertheless, to many it would have seemed that this was done by compulsion and against your will. Therefore now I preferred that this should in no case appear to anyone as forced, but, without doubt, voluntary.

1:15.t: For perhaps he departed for an hour for this reason, that you might receive him for ever: no longer as a slave, but instead of a slave a beloved brother, especially to me; but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord? Onesimus, having offended his own master, fled by a long journey to the Apostle, so as to show that he had not withdrawn in order to be liable for an offence, but so that, his sins blotted out, he might return useful to such a degree that he would not only become equal to his master in merits, but a brother also to the teacher himself. And lest Philemon, as is usual, should feel some disdain of pride, as a master against a slave, he humbles him when he calls him a brother both in the flesh and in the Lord; so that, the consideration of human condition being removed, since we are all from the one Adam, we may recognize ourselves as brothers: especially when faith comes between, which cuts off all pride.

He has well said, "perhaps," that the master may yield. For since the flight arose from perverseness, and a corrupt mind, and not from such intention, he has said, "perhaps." And he has not said, therefore he fled, but, therefore he was "separated," by a more fair sounding expression softening him the more. And he has not said, He separated himself, but, "he was separated." For it was not his own arrangement that he should depart either for this purpose or for that. Which also Joseph says, in making excuse for his brethren, "For God did send me hither" (Gen. xlv. 5), that is, He made use of their wickedness for a good end. "Therefore," he says, "he was parted for a season." Thus he contracts the time, acknowledges the offense, and turns it all to a providence. "That thou shouldest receive him," he says, "for ever," not for the present season only, but even for the future, that thou mightest always have him, no longer a slave, but more honorable than a slave. […]

For perhaps he therefore departed from you for an hour, that you might receive him eternal. No longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a dearest brother, especially to me: but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.

Sometimes evil becomes the occasion of good things, and God turns the crooked counsels of men to what is right. What I say will be made clearer by an example. Joseph's brothers, spurred on by the goads of their jealousy, sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty gold pieces (Gen. 37). This was the beginning of all good things for his father, for his brothers, and for all Egypt. Finally, he himself afterward said to his brothers: "You", he says, "thought evil things concerning me: and God thought good things concerning me" (Gen. 45:8). We can understand something similar in Onesimus too: evil beginnings were the occasions of a good thing. For if he had not run away from his master, he would never have come to Rome, where Paul was a prisoner in prison. […]

That you might receive him eternal. No one is the eternal master of his slave: for his power, and the condition of each of them, is ended by death. But Onesimus, who was made eternal through the faith of Christ, having received the spirit of liberty, began, from a slave, to be no longer a slave but a brother to Philemon, who is eternal because he too had believed in Christ: a dearest brother, an eternal brother; also to the eternal Apostle himself and to his master, to whom, as the condition of the flesh joined Onesimus before, so afterward the spirit joins him. And indeed then, when he was subject to him in the flesh, he was not joined to him in the Lord; but now he is joined to him both in the flesh and in the Lord. From this we understand that a slave who has believed in Christ is bound to his master by a twofold law: he is joined to him for a time by the necessity of the flesh, and united to him forever by the spirit.

Since Onesimus has changed his mind from being a wicked one, he himself turns it to the doubtful, as if he said: For perhaps he fled for reasons of caution.

"for this reason he was separated". With a euphemistic name, Paul called it separation, so that the memory of the separation would not provoke the master. Then he also limits the time, calming the anger, or he speaks in terms of a season of the year.

"so that you might have him back forever", you have, that is, you receive.

"But more than a slave". Do you see that escaping brought many benefits? For instead of an hour of escape, you have an eternal one. (For the escape is but one hour compared to eternity.) And instead of a worthless slave, you have received "a beloved brother".

"how much more to you". If to me, much more to you, even in worldly services. For this is "in the flesh." And in spiritual matters. For this is "in the Lord."

Since Onesimus ran away with evil intent, Paul turns this flight into something beneficial. Perhaps, he says, he ran away by the providence of God. He also commendably calls the flight a separation, so as not to irritate the master with the word "flight." And by shortening the time, he calms his anger. "For an hour," he says, "he was separated." At the same time he also shows that however long he was with Paul, he was also with Philemon. Therefore he was absent only for the time he spent before meeting Paul; and this is an insignificant amount of time, as if a single hour. Therefore from now on, if he, having been released by you, remains with me, then understand that he is serving you.

"To receive him back forever." You will make use of it.

1:16.t: Much, he says, benefit the flight brought: instead of one hour, you have him forever. For even the whole life of a man, in comparison with eternity, is nothing; much more so the time of flight. So instead of a slave, receive a brother; instead of an unprofitable one — a beloved one; "both in the flesh," that is, even in worldly matters he is worthy of love, as one who is serviceable, "and in the Lord," that is, in spiritual matters.

1:17.t: If then you hold me as a partner, receive him as me. He shows that he has such affection for Onesimus that he calls Philemon, whom he praises above, his sharer only if he receives this man as he would the Apostle. For this is what Solomon said: Free men will serve a wise slave (Sir. 10:28). This saying is meant to make Philemon fear, so that he might receive him at least for this reason, if he could not be moved by love.

No procedure is so apt to gain a hearing, as not to ask for everything at once. For see after how many praises, after how much preparation he hath introduced this great matter. After having said that he is "my son," that he is a partaker of the Gospel, that he is "my bowels," that thou receivest him back "as a brother," and "hold him as a brother," then he has added "as myself." And Paul was not ashamed to do this. For he who was not ashamed to be called the servant of the faithful, but confesses that he was such, much more would he not refuse this. But what he says is to this effect. If thou art of the same mind with me, if thou runnest upon the same terms, if thou considerest me a friend, receive him as myself.

If therefore you have me as a partner, receive him as me.

Philemon desired to have Paul as a partner, and, believing in Christ, he certainly wished to make such progress as to become like Paul and to share with him in his chains. Let us consider, therefore, how greatly Onesimus is praised here, and how far he is said to have progressed: for he is to be received as the Apostle is, and his master ought to desire his companionship just as he desires Paul's. In brief, what he says is this: If you wish to have me as a companion, have Onesimus too, whom I hold as my companion, and my son, and my bowels; if you do not receive him and are unwilling to have him, you yourself understand that you cannot have me.

"So if you consider me a partner". That is, if you think and wish the same things as I do.

"welcome him as you would me". Wow, how great is the magnitude of those words!
That is, if you acknowledge that you are of one mind with me, then receive him as you would me. Who would not be put to shame by the apostle? Who would not desire to receive Paul?

1:18.t: But if he has wronged you in anything, or is a debtor, charge this to me. Now he tears away the excuse of anger, lest perhaps Philemon should complain that he had been so wronged by him that he seemed by no means to deserve pardon. But if it were so, he says that it is to be charged to himself, through whom those who sinned before are to be heirs of the kingdom of heaven.

"If he hath wronged thee at all." See where and when he has introduced the mention of the injury; last, after having said so many things in his behalf. For since the loss of money is particularly apt to annoy men, that he might not accuse him of this, (for it was most likely that it was spent,) then he brings in this, and says, "If he hath wronged thee." He does not say, If he has stolen anything; but what? "If he hath wronged thee." At the same time he both confessed the offense, and not as if it were the offense of a servant, but of a friend against a friend, making use of the expression of "wrong" rather than of theft.

"Put that to mine account," he says, that is, reckon the debt to me, "I will repay it." Then also with that spiritual pleasantry, "I Paul write it with mine own hand." At once movingly and pleasantly; if when Paul did not refuse to execute a bond for him, he should refuse to receive him! This would both shame Philemon into compliance, and bring Onesimus out of trouble. "I write it," he says, "with mine own hand." Nothing is more affectionate than these "bowels," nothing more earnest, nothing more zealous. See what great concern he bestows in behalf of one man. "Albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides." Then that it might not appear insulting to him, whom he requests, if he had not the confidence to ask and obtain in behalf of a theft, he in some measure relieves this, saying, "That I say not unto thee how thou owest to me even thine own self besides." Not only thine own things, but thyself also. […]

But if he has harmed you in anything, or owes you, charge this to me.

He imitates his Lord and has Christ speaking in him, so he ought to do, as far as his strength allows, the things that Christ does. For if He bore our infirmities and grieved over our wounds, the Apostle rightly puts himself forward on behalf of Onesimus and pledges to pay what Onesimus owed. But, as we said above, the whole of it is what was taken by theft and squandered in luxury and could not be repaid. Philemon weighed this against a great price: in return for a runaway slave and money lost, he would receive both a dearest brother and an eternal brother, and through him he would make the Apostle his debtor.

"And if he has wronged you". Paul did not say, "He stole," but the verb is cut short. He says he "wronged" "or owes".

"charge that to me". For it was likely that they themselves had consumed together the things that had been stolen, and Paul says, "charge this to me," that is, charge these things as a debt to me, let the obligation be held against me.

"I, Paul, write". He wrote with spiritual grace, as if he said, But for safe keeping, that I will repay the debt, I have made the letters with my own hand.

"to avoid saying to you that you owe me your own self as well". So that Paul may not seem to insult him by not daring to appeal to him openly on behalf of the runaway slave (for this would show Philemon to be somewhat harsh), it shows that Paul is also very confident in Philemon. For he says not only your own things, but also yourself you owe to me.
He did not say: stole, but more gently: "wronged, or owes anything." It is likely that he had spent what was stolen. Therefore he says: charge it to my account, consider me the debtor.

1:19.t: I, Paul, have written with my own hand: I will repay; not to say to you that you owe me even your own self. If there is any offence on the part of Onesimus, he testifies that his own bond is sufficient to make satisfaction for him. And to speak the truth, he draws himself up and says that he demands less from him than he is proved to owe. For in the case of the slave he is compelled to make satisfaction, because he burdens himself with the debt.

I Paul have written with my own hand. I will repay, not to say to you that you owe me even your own self.

What he says amounts to this: What Onesimus carried off by theft, I pledge that I will repay. Of this pledge this Epistle is witness, and so is my own hand, for I did not dictate it in the usual way but wrote it out myself with my own hand. Believe me, therefore, when I make a promise on behalf of Onesimus. But I say this as though speaking to a stranger. Otherwise, if I return to my own right: because of the word of Christ which I preached to you as the Gospel, and you were made a Christian, you owe me your own self. But if you are mine, then all that is yours is also mine: Onesimus too, who is yours, is mine. I could therefore have used him as my own; but I leave it to your will, so that you may have a reward by pardoning.

He says this excellently, writing with spiritual grace and as if saying: for greater assurance that I will pay the debt, my own handwritten letter serves as guarantee.

Lest it seem reproachful to Philemon that the apostle, as though not trusting him, does not simply ask him concerning the slave-thief, but also gives a written guarantee in his own hand — for this would signal that Philemon is hard-hearted and inattentive to his teacher — the apostle (by the words cited) gives him to understand that he trusts him, and greatly so. For not only with your own possessions, he says, but beyond that, you owe me even your very self.

1:20.t: Even so, brother, so may I enjoy you in the Lord: refresh my heart in Christ. Having confidence in your obedience I have written to you, knowing that you will do beyond what I say. Now he coaxes him, so that his obedience may be voluntary, that he may be able to have its fruit. For thus he provokes him to do more than is asked of him; for it usually happens that one who sees that good is thought of him shows himself better.

What is, "Yea, brother"? Receive him, he says. For this we must understand though unexpressed. For dismissing all pleasantry, he again pursues his former considerations, that is, serious ones. And yet even these are serious. For the things that proceed from Saints are of themselves serious, even when they are pleasantry.
"Yea, brother, let me have joy of thee in the Lord, refresh my heart in Christ." That is, thou grantest the favor to the Lord, not to me. "My heart," that is, toward thyself.

Yes, brother, may I enjoy you in the Lord.

The Latin tongue does not render the Greek idiom. For in what he says, ναὶ, ἀδελφέ, ναὶ is a kind of adverb, as it were, of one who speaks coaxingly. But we, in translating it yes (ita), brother, give out a sound that is somehow more watery and diluted, something rather other than what is written. For just as that Hebrew ANNA (אנה), for which the Seventy translators frequently rendered ὦ δή, signifies in its own language the feeling of one who entreats (whence Symmachus sometimes rendered ANNA as δέομαι, that is, "I beseech"), so we too suffer the same strain with the Greek language that the Greeks endure with the Hebrew. But what he says, may I enjoy you in the Lord, is understood as something far different from what is supposed. The Apostle enjoys no one except him who has in himself many virtues in harmony with one another, and all that Christ is called according to the variety of occasions: namely wisdom, justice, continence, gentleness, temperance, chastity. […]

But when you have joy of a man in God, it is God rather than man that you enjoy. For you enjoy Him by whom you are made happy, and you rejoice to have come to Him in whose presence you place your hope of joy. And accordingly, Paul says to Philemon, "Yea, brother, let me have joy of thee in the Lord." For if he had not added "in the Lord," but had only said, "Let me have joy of thee," he would have implied that he fixed his hope of happiness upon him, although even in the immediate context to "enjoy" is used in the sense of to "use with delight." For when the thing that we love is near us, it is a matter of course that it should bring delight with it. And if you pass beyond this delight, and make it a means to that which you are permanently to rest in, you are using it, and it is an abuse of language to say that you enjoy it. But if you cling to it, and rest in it, finding your happiness complete in it, then you may be truly and properly said to enjoy it. […]

"Yes, brother". Again, from what is pleasing it advances to what is serious. "Yes," he said, "brother." What? Accept it yourself. I will take advantage from you in things that are according to Christ.

"May I enjoy". That is, I delight in your excellent works in the Lord. May I see you growing rich in all spiritual blessings.

"refresh my heart". Paul says, Refresh my love for you for the sake of Christ.

From heartfelt speech the apostle again passed to something more important, imploring: "let me have joy," he says, "of thee," that is, let me enjoy thy good deeds, not in worldly matters, but in those which are in the Lord.

Give rest, he says, to my love for you, or my heart for Christ's sake. For it is not to me that you do a kindness, but to Christ.

1:21.t: "Having confidence in thy obedience, I write unto thee." What stone would not these things have softened? What wild beast would not these things have rendered mild, and prepared to receive him heartily? After having borne witness to him by so many great testimonies of his goodness, he is not ashamed again to excuse himself. He says, Not barely requesting it, nor as commanding it, nor arbitrarily, but "having confidence in thy obedience I wrote unto thee." What he had said at the beginning, "having confidence," that he also says here in the sealing up of his letter.

"Knowing that thou wilt also do more than I say." At the same time in saying this he excited him. For he would have been ashamed, though for nothing else, if having such credit with him as this, that he would do more than he said,-he should not do so much.

Confident of your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even beyond what I say.

He who presumes upon the one he is about to ask in some way forestalls him by that very presumption, so that he is not free to refuse what is asked. Moreover, if the one who makes the request knows that the person asked will do more than he asked, he asks for lesser things for this reason: so that the one asked may have a voluntary reward, and one made greater by what he performs. But if Philemon does these things at a man's command, how much more will he do them for the love of God? Hence he is deservedly praised by the voice of the Apostle, because he anticipates his commands in deed and can say: "Let the voluntary offerings of my mouth be pleasing to you, O Lord" (Ps. 118:108); and because, doing more than was commanded, he surpasses those who did only what they were ordered, and who are bidden to say: "We are unprofitable servants; what we ought to have done, we have done" (Luke 17:10). […]

"confident". Paul said, "You do this not for me, but for Christ."

"confident in your obedience". I did not write to you as one commanding or stubbornly dealing with you, but having confidence "in your obedience". Whom would these things not soften, even if he were made of iron?

"knowing that you will also do more than I say". Paul said this, persuading Philemon in every way to accept Onesimus, if not for any other reason, then at least so as not to destroy his own reputation if he had any with the Apostle.
I, he says, wrote to you, not commanding and not out of self-love, but hoping in your obedience. What iron would not be softened by these words?

1:22.t: But at the same time prepare a lodging for me as well; for I hope that through your prayers I shall be given to you. To make him more careful and more obedient, he indicates that he is going to come to him; for the absent are wont to be despised. And why does the Apostle not disdain to be still here, he who always suffered wearinesses and deadly perils, beatings, persecutions and chains, and whose rest was nowhere but in Christ alone? But for the advancement of believers, and that he might confound the enemies of the cross of Christ so as to increase the glory of God, he offered his flesh to sufferings, that he might acquire crowns of immortality for his soul and his body.

"But withal prepare me also a lodging: for I trust that through your prayers I shall be given unto you." This also was the part of one who was exceedingly confident-or rather this too was in behalf of Onesimus, that not being indifferent, but knowing that he upon his return would know the things relating to him, they might lay aside all remembrance of the wrong, and might the rather grant the favor. For great was the influence and the honor of Paul residing among them, of Paul in his age, of Paul after imprisonment. Again, it is a proof of their love that he says that they pray; and to attribute to them so much as that they pray for "him." For although I be now in danger, yet nevertheless you will see me if ye pray for it.

At the same time, also prepare me a lodging.

I do not think the Apostle was so rich, or so encumbered with baggage, that he needed a lodging prepared for him. Nor do I think he was not content with a single little cell, he who would think a house small by the measure of his body most spacious. He says this rather so that, while Philemon expects him to come to him, he may all the more do what he has been asked. But if anyone thinks that this was commanded not by way of accommodation but in earnest, that a lodging should be prepared for him, then the lodging must be prepared for the apostle rather than for Paul. He was about to come to a new city, to preach the Crucified, and to bring doctrines never heard before, and he knew that very many would flock to him. It was therefore necessary, first, that the house be in a frequented part of the city, where people could easily gather. Next, that it be free of every disturbance; that it be ample, to hold a great many hearers; […]

"prepare a lodging for me". Paul says that he did not write only because of Onesimus (for Philemon would have said, if not for himself, that I was not worthy of even a word), but also for this reason, he says, that you might "prepare a lodging for me". And Philemon was even afraid that if he did not receive Onesimus, the Apostle would come and it would be known that he had been disobedient.

"for I hope that through your prayers". Great indeed is the power of prayers, and great also is the humility of Paul, because he was in need of those prayers.

It might have occurred to Philemon: if it were not for Onesimus, you would not have deemed me worthy of even a word. The Apostle heals this in advance, saying: I wrote not for his sake only, but also to ask you to prepare me a lodging; and at the same time, also to frighten him, because the Apostle will come and condemn him if he does not receive Onesimus.

Two things we learn from this: first, how great is the power of prayer, if even the great Paul needs their help; second, that one must be humble, if Paul needs the prayers of his disciples.

1:23.t: Epaphras, my fellow captive in Christ Jesus, greets you: Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Luke, my helpers. All these he testifies are sharers of his glory.

"Epaphras, my fellow-prisoner in Christ Jesus, saluteth thee." He was sent by the Colossians, so that from this it appears that Philemon was also at Colossae. And he calls him his "fellow-prisoner," showing that he also was in much tribulation, so that if not on his own account, yet on account of the other, it was right that he should be heard. For he that is in tribulation, and overlooks himself, and is concerned for others, deserves to be heard.

And he puts him to shame from another consideration, if his countryman is a fellow-prisoner with Paul and suffers affliction with him, and he himself does not grant him a favor in behalf of his own servant. And he has added, "my fellow-prisoner in Christ Jesus," instead of on account of Christ.

There are one or two more things on which he wishes condemnation to be passed. One is this: that these men say that the body is a prison, and like a chain round the soul; and that they assert that the soul does not depart, but returns to the place where it originally was. Let me give quotations to show his opinion on this point also.... And in the Commentary on Paul's Epistle to Philemon, at the place where he says "Epaphras my fellow-prisoner greeteth you," some way down he says: "Possibly, however, as some think, a more recondite and mysterious view is set before us, namely, that the two companions had been captured and bound and brought down into this vale of tears." You see how he represents these opinions as things which are held as a kind of esoteric mystery by certain persons, of whom, however, he is one.

Epaphras my fellow captive in Christ Jesus greets you, he says. As to who Epaphras, Paul's fellow captive, may be, we have received the following story. They say that the parents of the Apostle Paul were from the district of Gischala in Judea. When the whole province was being laid waste by the Roman hand and the Jews were being scattered across the world, they were removed to Tarsus, a city of Cilicia, and the young Paul followed his parents' lot. In this way, they say, what he testifies of himself can stand: "They are Hebrews, so am I: they are Israelites, so am I: they are the seed of Abraham, so am I" (2 Cor. 11:22). And again elsewhere: "A Hebrew of Hebrews" (Phil. 3:5), and the other things which mark him as a Jew rather than a man of Tarsus. If this is so, we can suppose that Epaphras too was taken captive at the same time that Paul was taken, and that, having been settled with his parents at Colossae, a city of Asia, he afterwards received the word of Christ. […]

Epaphras my fellow captive in Christ Jesus greets you: Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Luke, my fellow workers.

What we were saying at the beginning, that the Epistle to the Colossians was written at the same time and through the same bearer of the letters as the letter to Philemon, is also shown by the names of those who are introduced as sending greetings. For in that Epistle too it is written thus: "Aristarchus my fellow captive greets you, and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, and Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ" (Col. 4:10, 12); and a little further on: "Luke the dearest physician greets you, and Demas; and say to Archippus: See the ministry which you have received in the Lord, that you fulfil it" (ibid. 14, 17); and: "Be mindful of my chains" (ibid. 18). But suppose someone thinks that they were not written together, because the Epistle to the Colossians has a few names that are not found written here. […]

"Epaphras, my fellow prisoner". This man was sent from the Colossians to Paul, as it is clear that Philemon was from Colossae. He is called a fellow prisoner, indicating that he too was in great distress. Moreover, this also honors him; for Epaphras was indeed a fellow prisoner, whereas this one did not even show kindness to Onesimus, who was a prisoner for the Lord.

This Epaphras was sent to Paul by the Colossians; from this it is clear that Philemon was from Colossae. He calls him "fellow prisoner," showing that Epaphras too was in great distress, thereby making Philemon feel that if Epaphras suffers with Paul, will Philemon really not show mercy to Onesimus for his sake? "Fellow prisoner," he says, not for any human reason, but for the sake of Christ Jesus, suffering together with me for the Gospel.

1:24.t: "Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Luke, my fellow-workers." Why then does he put Luke last? And yet he elsewhere says, "Only Luke is with me" (2 Tim. iv. 11), and "Demas," he says, was one of those who "forsook him, having loved the present world." (2 Tim. iv. 10.) All these things, although they are mentioned elsewhere, yet nevertheless ought not to be passed over here without enquiry, nor ought we merely to hear them as things of course. But how comes he to say that he who forsook him salutes them? For "Erastus," he says, "abode at Corinth." (2 Tim. iv. 20.) He adds Epaphras, both as known to them, and being of their country. And Mark, as being himself also an admirable man. Why then does he number Demas with these? Perhaps it was after this that he became more remiss, when he saw the dangers multiplied. But Luke being last became first. And from these indeed he salutes him, urging him the more to obedience, and calls them his fellow-laborers, and in this way shames him into granting the request.

As for the rest, in writing the letter to Philemon he names as fellow workers in the Gospel and in his chains Mark, whom I take to be the writer of the Gospel; and Aristarchus, whom we mentioned above; and Demas, of whom he complains in another place: "Demas has forsaken me, loving the present world, and has gone to Thessalonica". And he names Luke the physician, who, in leaving the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles to the churches, was turned from a physician of bodies into a physician of souls, just as the apostles were made from fishers of fish into fishers of men (Matt. 4). Of him it is said in another place also: "I have sent", he says, "with him the brother whose praise is in the Gospel through all the churches" (2 Cor. 8:18). As often as his book is read in the churches, so often his medicine does not cease.

"Aristarchus, Demas". About this, Paul wrote to Timothy, "Demas abandoned me." (2 Tim. 4:10)

[PHOTIUS] They say that this Demas again turned away to Hellenism and became a priest of idols. [end of the Photius excerpt]

[OECUMENIUS] And if that was at first, now he has repented. But if later, after these things he became negligent. [end of the excerpt by Oecumenius]

"Luke". The last became first. For if in the second letter to Timothy he says, Luke is the only one with me. (2 Tim. 4:11) And he calls them "co-workers", showing that these also, he says, are encouraging you with me.

Demas at first enjoyed respect, as is attested here concerning him as a fellow worker of Paul, but afterwards through frivolity he fell away from Paul, as indeed Paul writes about this in the epistle to Timothy, written evidently after this epistle. "For Demas has forsaken me; only Luke is with me" (2 Tim. 4:9). Thus Luke, placed here last, became first of all when Demas fell away. So no one should place hope in himself, but let him who stands take heed lest he fall. By saying "fellow worker," he shows that they too together with me ask you, and it is worthy to show favorable attention to such persons.

1:25.t: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, amen. This is the subscription of the Apostle, confirming the letter he has sent.

"The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen."

He hath closed his Epistle with a prayer. And indeed prayer is a great good, salutary, and preservative of our souls. But it is great when we do things worthy of it, and do not render ourselves unworthy. And thou too, therefore, when thou goest to the priest, and he shall say to thee, "The Lord will have mercy on thee, my son," do not confide in the word only, but add also works. Do acts worthy of mercy, God will bless thee, my son, if indeed thou doest things worthy of blessing. He will bless thee, if thou showest mercy to thy neighbor. For the things which we wish to obtain from God, of those we ought first to impart to our neighbors. But if we deprive our neighbors of them, how can we wish to obtain them? "Blessed," He says, "are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy." For if men show mercy to such, much more will God, but to the unmerciful by no means. "For he shall have judgment without mercy to him that hath showed no mercy."

Grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.

Just as the people of Israel is numbered by the better part of man, the head, as Scripture says, according to their heads (Num. 1:2), so the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ is indeed in the whole man and in every part of the saints. But by synecdoche it is said of the whole man, from the greater and better part, that is, the spirit: Grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. And when grace is in the spirit, it makes the whole man spiritual, so that the flesh too serves the spirit, and the soul is not overcome by the flesh, and, brought together into a spiritual substance, cleaves to the Lord; for he who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit (1 Cor. 6).
